title: "Tutti Fratelli" at Solferino
text:
On 24 June 1859 the armies of France and Piedmont-Sardinia fought the Austrian army near the village of Solferino in northern Italy. It was one of the largest battles of the century, and by evening tens of thousands of men lay dead or wounded. The armies' medical services were completely overwhelmed.

A Swiss businessman, Henry Dunant, arrived that evening. He had come hoping to see Napoleon III about a business venture in Algeria. Instead he found himself in the nearby town of Castiglione delle Stiviere, where thousands of wounded soldiers had been carried into churches, houses and streets, many lying without water, food or care.

Dunant began organizing help. He gathered local women and girls to wash wounds, bring water and food, write letters for the dying and simply sit with them. He bought supplies with his own money and set up makeshift care in the main church. The women tended French, Italian and Austrian soldiers alike. In his account, Dunant reports that they repeated, "Tutti fratelli," all are brothers.

Back in Geneva, he wrote A Memory of Solferino, published in 1862, proposing that every country form volunteer relief societies in peacetime, ready to aid the wounded in war, and that nations agree to protect them. In 1863 a committee of five Geneva citizens, including Dunant, founded what became the International Committee of the Red Cross. The first Geneva Convention followed in 1864. In 1901 Dunant shared the first Nobel Peace Prize.
lesson: Volunteers who care for everyone in need, regardless of side, can start something far larger than themselves. Organized compassion lasts longer than individual pity.
people: Henry Dunant, the women of Castiglione delle Stiviere
location: Solferino and Castiglione delle Stiviere, Lombardy, Italy
source: Henry Dunant, A Memory of Solferino (Un souvenir de Solferino, 1862)
